First Timothy
furst TIM-oh-thee
noun (proper)
Named for its recipient, Timothy (Greek Timōtheus, “honoring God”) — Paul's younger co-worker and delegate at Ephesus; the first of two canonical letters to him is the primary New Testament source for church office qualifications, worship order, and the male-only teaching eldership.

Biblical Definition

The First Epistle to Timothy is one of the three Pastoral Epistles (with 2 Timothy and Titus), written by Paul from Macedonia after his release from first Roman imprisonment, circa AD 63–65. Timothy was stationed at Ephesus to correct doctrinal error (1 Tim 1:3) and order the congregation's institutional life. The letter addresses prayer and public worship (ch. 2), the office of overseer and deacon (ch. 3), the threat of apostate teaching (ch. 4), and the care of widows and elders (ch. 5). Its ecclesiological contributions are foundational for Reformed church order: the two-office structure (elder/overseer and deacon) with strict personal qualifications; and the male-only restriction on the teaching office — “But I do not allow a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man” (1 Tim 2:12), grounded not in Ephesian culture but in the order of creation: “For it was Adam who was first formed, and then Eve” (1 Tim 2:13). The church is “the pillar and support of the truth” (1 Tim 3:15) — a phrase that grounds the congregation's doctrinal responsibility in its constituted nature as the household of God. The overseer must be “above reproach — the husband of one wife, sober-minded, prudent, respectable, hospitable, able to teach” (1 Tim 3:2); these qualifications govern the Reformed tradition's officer examination from the Reformation to the present.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster does not record “First Timothy” as a common English noun; it is a proper designation for the first of Paul's two canonical letters to his co-worker Timothy, the foundational New Testament text for church office and worship order.

FIRST TIMOTHY, n. [From Timōtheus, a Greek personal name meaning ‘honoring God.’] The first canonical letter of the Apostle Paul to Timothy, his younger ministerial delegate stationed at Ephesus; one of the three Pastoral Epistles that constitute the New Testament's primary source for church government, ministerial qualifications, and the regulation of public worship.

The Reformers and Puritans relied on 1 Timothy for their articulation of church office: Calvin's Institutes IV.3, the Westminster Confession of Faith ch. 30, and the 1689 LBCF ch. 26 all draw on its two-office structure (elder and deacon) and its male-only teaching-elder restriction grounded in creation order.

The letter's definition of the church as “the pillar and support of the truth” (1 Tim 3:15) has been a cardinal text for Reformed ecclesiology: the local congregation is not a fellowship club or a voluntary association but the divinely constituted guardian of apostolic doctrine.

Key Scripture

1 Tim 2:12 — "But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence."

1 Tim 2:13 — "For Adam was first formed, then Eve."

1 Tim 3:2 — "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;"

1 Tim 3:15 — "But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth."

Modern Corruption

Egalitarian and progressive readings treat 1 Timothy 2:12 as a culturally conditioned local prohibition rather than a creational principle; critical scholars deny Pauline authorship of the Pastorals to sidestep their authority.

expand to see more

The two principal corruptions of First Timothy are exegetical and canonical. Exegetically, egalitarian interpreters (Philip Payne, I. Howard Marshall, CBE International) argue that 1 Tim 2:12's prohibition of women teaching or exercising authority is a local, situational response to a specific Ephesian error by unlearned women, not a binding creational ordinance. This requires reading Paul's explicit grounding in creation order (v. 13–14) as merely illustrative rather than foundational — a hermeneutical maneuver the text itself resists. Paul does not appeal to Ephesian culture but to Adam's priority in creation and Eve's primacy in the transgression; both warrant the prohibition's permanent scope.

Canonically, critical scholars (Martin Dibelius, Jürgen Roloff, the “Deutero-Pauline” school) deny Pauline authorship of the Pastorals, attributing them to a late-first-century Pauline school writing in his name. This removes their apostolic authority and allows 1 Tim 2:12 to be dismissed as post-Pauline churchly conservatism. The Reformed confessional tradition holds Pauline authorship of all 13 epistles bearing his name on the basis of their own claims, early patristic attestation, and canonical standing. The denial of Pauline authorship is not a neutral scholarly finding but a dogmatic commitment to the historical-critical paradigm, which the dictionary's voice-lock rejects.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in the personal name Timothy (Greek Timōtheus) and the ecclesiological vocabulary of the New Testament — episkopos (overseer), diakonos (deacon), and presbyteros (elder) — the three terms First Timothy deploys to structure the local church.

expand to see more

Greek Timōtheus (Τιμόθεος) — Timothy, “one who honors God”; Paul's most intimate co-worker (Acts 16:1), son in the faith (1 Tim 1:2), and delegate to troubled churches including Ephesus and Corinth

Greek episkopos (ἐπίσκοπος) — overseer, bishop; in 1 Tim 3:1–7 interchangeable with elder and pastor, defining one office with plural functions: teaching, ruling, and guarding the flock

Greek diakonos (διάκονος) — deacon, servant; the second church office in 1 Tim 3:8–13, distinguished from the elder by its service rather than teaching-and-ruling function

Greek didaskein (διδάσκειν) — to teach; the verbal form whose restriction in 1 Tim 2:12 has governed the Reformed tradition's male-only teaching eldership across five centuries of confessional church practice

Greek stylos kai hedraiōma — pillar and support (1 Tim 3:15); the image that burdens the local church with custodianship of the truth — not a private fellowship but the institutional guardian of the apostolic deposit

Usage

"First Timothy 3:1–7 is the Reformed tradition's standard elder-examination checklist: the qualifications are not aspirational ideals but minimum criteria — a man who fails any of them is disqualified from the office regardless of his gifts or popularity."

"The grounding of the teaching restriction in creation order (1 Tim 2:13) rather than Ephesian culture establishes its trans-cultural, permanent scope: it does not admit revision by changing social customs because its warrant precedes custom by millennia."

"First Timothy's two-office structure (overseer and deacon) is the biblical norm against which the Reformed tradition measures every church polity: episcopalianism adds a third officer above Scripture's warrant; congregationalism without plural elders lacks the oversight the letter requires."
